Alcohol-related impairments

One mouse study found better cognitive and spatial-memory performance and fewer reactive hippocampal astrocytes after near-infrared PBM following chronic adolescent alcohol exposure.

1unique publication

Publication and study types

Mouse experiment: 1

No human or in-vitro study identified

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for cognitive and hippocampal tissue outcomes in one mouse model

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One mouse study found better cognitive and spatial-memory performance and fewer reactive hippocampal astrocytes after near-infrared PBM following chronic adolescent alcohol exposure.

Summary of the Evidence

One unique publication is classified directly under alcohol-related impairments. It is a controlled mouse experiment involving chronic alcohol exposure during adolescence. The category contains no human treatment study, and it should be kept distinct from alcohol-addiction treatment studies, methanol toxicity, and alcohol-related liver conditions.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study of PBM for alcohol-related cognitive impairment was identified in this category. There is therefore no patient evidence on memory, daily function, drinking behavior, or recovery after alcohol exposure.

Animal evidence

Hong et al. studied C57BL/6 mice exposed to ethanol during adolescence. The alcohol-exposed mice received 830 nm laser treatment five times a week for three weeks. Compared with untreated alcohol-exposed mice, the PBM group performed better on cognitive and spatial-memory tasks. The researchers also found fewer reactive astrocytes in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in learning and memory. These are two findings from the same experiment, not independent replications (Hong et al., 2025).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell-culture or ex-vivo experiment is classified for alcohol-related impairment. The astrocyte finding was measured in tissue from the same treated mice and is not a stand-alone cell study.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The mouse experiment used an 830-nm near-infrared laser; the database record does not identify the manufacturer or model. It reports an irradiance of 50 mW/cm² and 15 sessions over three weeks. The exposure time and fluence are not reported in the database record. This single animal protocol does not establish which settings would reach human brain tissue or whether a similar intervention would affect people with alcohol-related cognitive symptoms.

Interpretation

In this adolescent alcohol-exposure model, PBM improved memory-task performance and reduced a hippocampal glial marker. Both results point in a favorable direction within the experiment. With no human study and only one mouse publication, the findings establish a preclinical result rather than a clinical treatment effect.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The category contains one controlled mouse experiment, which reported improved memory-task performance and fewer reactive hippocampal astrocytes after PBM. It provides a direction of effect in a specific adolescent alcohol-exposure model, but there is no human replication or clinical outcome. Independent animal replication followed by carefully controlled studies in people with alcohol-related cognitive impairment would be needed for a stronger rating.
